newsitem.title: USA: Clinton focuses on inner city problems.
newsitem.headline: Clinton focuses on inner city problems.

text.p: After a weekend of foreign policy, President Clinton Monday turned to the domestic scene, unveiling steps to encourage home ownership in inner cities as well as a privately funded children's health care program.

Making a 24-hour visit to California after the G7 summit in Denver, Clinton also planned to attend three fund-raisers to benefit the Democratic Party, deeply in debt from his 1996 re-election, and Sen. Barbara Boxer, a California Democrat.

At the Group of Seven (G7) Denver summit, which gathered leaders from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States as well as Russia, Clinton boasted that the U.S. economy was at its strongest in a generation.
On Monday he focused the spotlight on two sectors that have not seen the full fruits of surging U.S. growth: inner cities and the 10 million American children without health insurance.
Speaking in the morning to the U.S. Conference of Mayors in San Francisco, Clinton said American cities are in better shape because of the recovery but have not enjoyed its full benefits.
"We have got to keep working until we extend the prosperity of this recovery to every neighborhood in America," he said.

The White House timed Clinton's speech to co-incide with the release of a federal report that found cities facing three key problems: urban unemployment remains higher than suburban and national rates; the poor have become more concentrated in inner cities, and middle class city flight continues.
Clinton announced three steps to help people buy homes in inner cities:

-- The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) will begin a one-year program to make it cheaper for police officers to buy homes in the neighborhoods where they work by allowing them to buy HUD-foreclosed properties for half price. HUD hopes 1,000 police officers will take up the offer.

-- The Federal Housing Administration will cut its mortgage insurance premiums by 25 basis points to 1.5 percent for first time homebuyers in the largest U.S. cities, saving them $200 on an average $85,000 mortgage.
-- The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. will begin a test program to help up to 2,000 low-income people buy homes by allowing them to use their Section 8 federal rent subsidies for mortgage payments.
HUD Secretary Andrew Cuomo told reporters that the three programs would cost the government $700 million annually and said the funds would come from within HUD's budget.

The small-scale measures were characteristic of Clinton's second-term proposals, where he has looked for initiatives that require little new federal money at a time when the government is seeking to eliminate the federal budget deficit by 2002.

In another such initiative, Clinton flew to Los Angeles later in the day to announce that a private company, Kaiser Permanente, would spend $100 million to provide health care coverage to up to 50,000 uninsured children in California.

The not-for-profit company said it would spend the money over five years to fund insurance for children from low-income families as well as to sign up children who are eligible for state health insurance but are not enrolled.

Clinton was scheduled to attend three fund-raisers during the day -- two to raise about $1.5 million for Boxer, who is expected to face a tough and expensive re-election fight in 1998 -- and one to bring in $80,000 for the Democratic Party.
